title: Quantitative Prediction of Long-Term Precipitation Hardening in Type 316 Stainless Steel Welds Using a Hybrid FEM-Neural Network System
abstract: Abstract The stress corrosion cracking (SCC) susceptibility of the weld heat-affected zone (HAZ) in austenitic stainless steels used in nuclear power plants is influenced by several factors such as residual tensile stress, hardness of materials, and environment. This study focuses on low-temperature precipitation hardening (LTPH) due to M 23 C 6  carbide formation in the multi-pass weld HAZ of SUS316 steel during long-term operation. A hybrid prediction system was developed by integrating systematic isothermal aging experiments (300 °C to 500 °C, up to 2000 hours), parametric analysis using the Larson-Miller parameter (LMP), and a neural network (NN) model. The NN model, trained on data across a range of pre-strains (5 to 30 pct), successfully captures the non-linear effects of local strain, thermal history, and nucleation condition on LTPH amount (ΔHV). By coupling this NN model with finite element method (FEM) simulations of multi-pass welding, the spatial distribution of LTPH across the entire HAZ after long-term aging can be predicted. This hybrid FEM-NN approach enables quantitative prediction of the spatial distribution of long-term intragranular hardening in the HAZ of austenitic stainless steels, thereby providing a valuable tool for integrity assessment during long-term plant operation.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Austenitic stainless steels, particularly type 316 (SUS316), are widely used in welded structures for high-temperature applications such as chemical plants, nuclear reactor components, and thermal power plants due to their excellent corrosion resistance and mechanical properties. [ 1 ]  However, the long-term soundness of welded joints in these environments remains of concern in general. The heat-affected zone (HAZ) of multi-pass welds for high-temperature applications can be susceptible to several hardening mechanisms that may lead to reduced toughness and increased stress corrosion cracking susceptibility, due to strain hardening, dynamic strain aging during multi-pass welding, and precipitation hardening during long-term aging. [ 2 ]

Although the hardening mechanisms in HAZ of austenitic stainless steels associated with the welding thermal cycle have been somewhat studied, the role of precipitation hardening during long-term aging at relatively low temperatures (300 °C to 500 °C) has rarely been considered systematically. It is widely believed that large-scale precipitation of carbides (primarily M 23 C 6 ) in austenitic stainless steel occurs only above approximately 600 °C. [ 3 ]  However, recent studies have demonstrated that fine M 23 C 6  carbides can precipitate at temperatures as low as 300 °C in strained microstructures, resulting in measurable hardening over time. [ 4 ]  Vitek and David specifically showed that this phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the heat-affected zone (HAZ), where the plastic strain field generated by welding provides abundant dislocation networks that serve as preferential nucleation sites for M 23 C 6  carbides, thereby accelerating precipitation kinetics. [ 5 ]  In nuclear power plants, components operate at elevated temperatures. Staehle and Gorman comprehensively reviewed the operating conditions of light water reactors and identified the temperature ranges of 280 °C to 300 °C for BWRs and approximately 300 °C for PWRs as critical for SCC susceptibility. [ 6 ]  Andresen and Ford established the fundamental understanding of SCC crack growth rate dependencies on environmental and material parameters in these reactor environments. [ 7 ]  Johnson and Allen provided a technical basis for evaluating material degradation under extended service, reporting the operational temperature ranges relevant to this study. [ 8 ]  These conditions are reflected in the design requirements of the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code. [ 9 ]  Therefore, the precipitation hardening at low temperature around 300 °C is highly relevant to nuclear power plant components that experience long-term service at reactor operating temperatures.

In our previous study, [ 10 ]  the authors experimentally confirmed the existence of low-temperature precipitation hardening (LTPH) in the simulated heat-affected zone of SUS316 at low temperatures (300 °C to 500 °C). The main findings included the following: (A) the pre-strained material without pre-existing carbide nuclei exhibited initial recovery softening followed by hardening due to M 23 C 6  precipitation, while the pre-strained material with pre-existing carbide nuclei hardened immediately due to accelerated carbide nucleation and growth; (B) transmission electron microscopy (TEM) identified precipitates inside the grains and at the grain boundaries as M 23 C 6  carbides; (C) the kinetics of carbide precipitation were directly correlated with the observed increase in hardness; and (D) the hardening mechanism was considered to be classical precipitation strengthening, where the precipitated M 23 C 6  particles inhibit dislocation movement. These findings provide a basic microstructural and mechanistic basis for understanding LTPH.

Despite the aforementioned basic understanding, a critical gap remains in translating these laboratory-scale research findings into practical, long-term engineering predictions for nuclear power plant components operating at approximately 300 °C. The kinetics of LTPH during decades of service (typical plant design life of 40 to 60 years, with potential extension to 80–100 years), its spatial distribution in the complex strain gradient of the multi-pass weld HAZ, and a quantitative framework for predicting the hardening increments under actual reactor operating temperatures have not yet been established. Traditional time–temperature parameter (TTP) approaches, such as the Larson-Miller parameter (LMP), [ 11 ]  are effective for extrapolating properties like creep rupture, residual stress relaxation, and tempering, but have not been systematically applied to low-temperature precipitation hardening in welded microstructures at nuclear service temperatures. Furthermore, the spatial prediction of the properties in heterogeneous weld regions requires advanced modeling techniques to integrate the effects of multiple variables, such as local strain and thermal history. [ 12 , 13 ]

To fill this gap, the present study focuses on the following objectives: To systematically quantify the long-term hardening behavior caused by LTPH at temperatures relevant to nuclear reactor operation (300 °C to 500 °C) and construct hardness evolution curves on the basis of kinetic modeling for precipitation hardening. To develop a generalized quantitative prediction model for LTPH by using LMP, enabling extrapolation to service lives of plants for several decades (up to 100 years). To construct a neural network (NN)-based prediction system that considers the key influences of local strain, temperature, and time on LTPH kinetics, creating a database-driven model for heterogeneous microstructures. To establish a hybrid prediction framework by integrating the strain field simulated by the finite element method (FEM) [ 14 ]  with the NN-based prediction system, enabling comprehensive numerical prediction of the LTPH distribution in the HAZ of multi-pass welds during long-term operation ( e.g. , 300 °C for 40 to 100 years).

This study establishes a hybrid FEM-NN-based comprehensive quantitative framework for predicting the hardness increment due to LTPH in the weld HAZ of SUS316 stainless steel during long-term operation especially for nuclear power plants. This integration of computational mechanics (FEM) and artificial intelligence (NN) offers a new approach for assessing long-term microstructural degradation and directly contributes to the suitability assessment and remaining life prediction of critical welded components operating at service temperatures.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: A commercial SUS316 austenitic stainless steel was used as the base material. The welding wire was YS316, which has similar chemical compositions to SUS316, as listed in Table  I . The chemical composition of the SUS316 base material was confirmed by independent analysis using optical emission spectroscopy (OES) and inductively coupled plasma (ICP) mass spectrometry. Three independent measurements were performed on samples taken from different locations of the as-received plate. The measured values were within ± 5 pct of the certified values provided by the material supplier, confirming the composition listed in Table  I . The carbon content was further verified by combustion infrared absorption method (LECO CS230) to ensure accuracy at low concentration levels. sections.heading: Specimen Preparation and Heat Treatments
paragraphs: To systematically investigate the LTPH behavior and establish a comprehensive database for neural network training, two categories of SUS316 specimens were prepared.

For the mechanistic study focusing on the effect of pre-existing carbide nuclei, two material conditions were investigated, both pre-strained to 20 pct by cold rolling: Specimen A without pre-existing carbide nuclei,  and Specimen B with pre-existing carbide nuclei, which was subjected to a prior thermomechanical treatment to introduce fine carbide nuclei (as detailed in Reference  10 ).

To construct a reliable database covering a wide range of pre-strain levels for neural network training, additional specimens were prepared with cold rolling reductions varying from 5 to 30 pct. These specimens, encompassing both conditions without and with pre-existing carbide nuclei, were used to capture the influence of local strain on LTPH kinetics.
All specimens were subjected to isothermal aging treatments in an electric furnace over a temperature range of 300 °C to 500 °C for durations from 1 to 2000 hours, followed by water quenching.

sections.heading: Hardness Measurements
paragraphs: The thermally aged samples were subjected to intragranular Vickers hardness tests. The LTPH amount (ΔHV) was defined as the increase in hardness relative to the pre-aging condition for each material state. After polishing, the hardness of the test specimens was measured under a load of 0.49 N for 10 seconds using an HMV-G Micro Vickers Hardness Tester (Shimadzu Corp.). The maximum and minimum values were excluded from the multiple measurements, and the average hardness value was calculated.

sections.heading: Parametric analysis
paragraphs: Hardening data were analyzed using the Larson-Miller Parameter (LMP =  T  ( C  + log  t ), where  T  is temperature in Kelvin,  t  is time in hours, and  C  is a constant). A value of  C  = 20 was employed based on preliminary fitting.

sections.heading: Neural network (NN) model
paragraphs: A neural network model was constructed using a radial basis function (RBF). The input variables were pre-aging strain ( ε ), aging temperature ( T ), aging time ( t ), and nucleation condition (with/without carbide nuclei). The output variable was the LTPH increment (ΔHV). The experimental database was used to train the neural network model for predicting LTPH values. The NN model was validated using 5-fold cross-validation. The dataset was randomly partitioned into 5 subsets. Each subset was used once as the test set, while the remaining 4 subsets were used for training. The following metrics were calculated: coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE).

sections.heading: Finite element analysis
paragraphs: The strain distribution in the HAZ of a multi-pass welded SUS316 joint was calculated using finite element method (FEM) under relevant welding conditions. The equivalent plastic strain distribution at the end of the welding simulation was extracted as the “initial state” for subsequent long-term aging prediction.

sections.heading: Comprehensive prediction
paragraphs: The strain distribution from FEM and the long-term aging condition (for example, at 300 °C for 40, 60, and 100 years) were used as inputs to the trained NN model to predict the spatial distribution of the LTPH increment (ΔHV) and generate a full-field contour map of ΔHV throughout the entire HAZ.

sections.heading: Time–Temperature Dependence of Low-Temperature Precipitation Hardening (LTPH)
paragraphs: Following the confirmation of LTPH and its mechanism in our previous study, [ 10 ]  the hardening kinetics were systematically evaluated. The hardness evolution of both Specimen A (without pre-existing carbide nuclei) and Specimen B (with pre-existing carbide nuclei) was measured after isothermal aging at temperatures ranging from 300 °C to 500 °C for durations between 1 and 2000 hours. Figure  1  illustrates the time–temperature dependence of LTPH hardening curves for two material states. The net LTPH amount (ΔHV) was defined as the hardness increment attributable solely to LTPH, accounting for any initial recovery softening. Fig. 1 Time–temperature dependence of LTPH hardening curves

For Specimen A without pre-existing carbide nuclei, no significant hardening was observed after aging at 300 °C for up to 2000 hours. After thermal aging at 350 °C and above, hardening was observed, and the hardening amount increased monotonically with aging time. The LTPH amount (ΔHV) also increased with increasing thermal aging temperature.

In contrast, for Specimen B with pre-existing carbide nuclei, because carbides had already nucleated before thermal aging, hardening was observed immediately after thermal aging at temperatures above 300 °C, with the hardening amount also increasing monotonically with aging time and temperature. This confirms that the presence of pre-existing nuclei eliminates the incubation period for carbide precipitation, leading to accelerated hardening kinetics at lower temperatures.

Figure  2  shows a summary of the LTPH curves for both Specimen A and Specimen B based on the change in hardness after thermal aging at 300 °C to 500 °C (1 to 2000 hours). Based on these data, the LTPH phenomenon was confirmed after low-temperature thermal aging, and the hardening amount increased monotonically with holding time and temperature. Compared with Specimen A, the curves for Specimen B consistently showed an earlier hardening initiation point and a higher hardening rate, directly demonstrating the accelerative effect of pre-existing, strain-induced nucleation sites. Fig. 2 Summary of the LTPH hardening curves for Specimens A and B after thermal aging at 300 °C to 500 °C (1 to 2000 h)

sections.heading: Quantitative Prediction Formula for LTPH
paragraphs: The time–temperature equivalence for LTPH was effectively described using the LMP in Eq. [ 1 ]. LMP was proposed by Hollomon and Jaffe as a tempering parameter. For the change in hardness of austenitic stainless steel due to tempering,  C  is considered to be at or near 20. The  C  value is also often assumed to be close to 20 for creep. [ 18 ]  Therefore, in this study,  C  = 20 was used to analyze the relationship between LMP and the LTPH amount (ΔHV). The results are shown in Figure  3 . Fig. 3 The relationship between LMP and LTPH amount (ΔHV)

As presented in Figure  3 (a), in the absence of pre-existing carbide nuclei, the change in hardness after thermal aging occurs due to two phenomena: carbide nucleation and subsequent growth of carbides. The carbide nucleation event introduces a stochastic factor, disrupting the simple correlation with LMP. Therefore, there is no clear correlation between the LTPH amount and LMP. Conversely, as shown in Figure  3 (b), in the presence of pre-existing carbide nuclei, these nuclei have already formed, and hardening after thermal aging occurs due primarily to the growth of these pre-existing nuclei. Therefore, a correlation exists between the LTPH amount and LMP. Furthermore, the correlation coefficient of the curve fitting between the LTPH amount and LMP appears to be higher than that of the linear fitting.

The reason for this is that, as shown in Figure  4 , thermodynamic calculations using Thermo-Calc (TCFE9 database) show that as temperature increases from 300 °C to 600 °C, the composition of M 23 C 6  shifts from being Cr-rich toward containing more Fe. This variation in carbide chemistry with temperature might contribute to the non-linear (curvilinear) correlation between the LTPH amount and LMP, which provides a better fit than a simple linear relationship. Fig. 4 Thermo-Calc equilibrium calculation of M 23 C 6  phase behavior in SUS316 steel (TCFE9 database)

sections.heading: Neural Network-Based Model for LTPH Prediction Across the HAZ
paragraphs: In multi-pass welded joints, the local strain history and consequently the hardening behavior due to LTPH are not uniform throughout the HAZ. To capture this spatial heterogeneity and enable full-field prediction of LTPH distribution, a data-driven predictive model was developed using a Neural Network (NN).

sections.heading: Experimental database construction
paragraphs: A comprehensive database of LTPH amounts for Specimens A and B under various aging conditions, particularly under different pre-strain levels (simulating variations in HAZ location), was compiled to serve as the training database. The hardening behavior under these conditions is summarized in Figures  5  and  6 . Figure  5  shows the LTPH amount as a function of aging temperature and time for specimens without pre-existing carbide nuclei, while Figure  6  presents the corresponding results for specimens with pre-existing nuclei. These results show that under identical thermal aging conditions, the LTPH amount increased with increasing pre-strain. Furthermore, for a given strain level, the LTPH amount increased with both higher aging temperature and longer holding time. Fig. 5 Hardness increment of Specimen A (without carbide nuclei) after thermal aging under different initial strains Fig. 6 Hardness increment of Specimens B (with carbide nuclei) after thermal aging under different initial strains

sections.heading: Neural network architecture and training
paragraphs: To establish a quantitative relationship between the local thermomechanical history and the resulting hardening behavior, an empirical model was constructed using a radial basis function neural network (RBF-NN). [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]  The radial basis function neural network (RBF-NN) was selected for the following specific reasons: Non-linear mapping capability: The relationship between LTPH amount and input variables (strain, LMP, nucleation condition) exhibits strong non-linearity, particularly evident in the curvilinear correlation between ΔHV and LMP (Figure  3 ). RBF-NNs, with their Gaussian activation functions, are theoretically capable of approximating any continuous non-linear function to arbitrary accuracy given sufficient hidden neurons. [ 21 , 22 ] Faster training convergence: Unlike multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) that require iterative backpropagation, RBF-NNs employ a two-stage training process (unsupervised center determination followed by linear weight optimization), which typically converges faster and avoids local minima problems common in gradient-descent-based methods. Local approximation property: The localized nature of Gaussian basis functions makes RBF-NNs particularly suitable for problems where the input–output relationship is not globally uniform, as is the case here where nucleation condition causes fundamentally different hardening behaviors. This locality ensures that training data from one region of the input space does not unduly influence predictions in distant regions. Interpolation capability: Given the relatively sparse experimental data in certain regions of the parameter space, RBF-NNs provide smooth interpolation between training points without imposing global parametric assumptions.
The trained RBF-NN model accepts three input parameters:

The single output node returns the predicted LTPH amount (ΔHV). The network was trained using the compiled experimental database (Section III–C– 1 ). Through this training process, the model successfully learned the non-linear relationships governing precipitation hardening kinetics and their dependence on local strain and thermal history.

Equivalent plastic strain ( ε ): Representing the local strain from multi-pass welding. Larson–Miller Parameter (LMP): A combined time–temperature parameter, which consolidates the effects of aging temperature and time. Nucleation condition (Φ): A binary categorical variable indicating the initial microstructural state. Φ = 0 denotes material without pre-existing carbide nuclei, while Φ = 1 denotes material with pre-existing nuclei.

sections.heading: Model output and predictive capability
paragraphs: The trained NN model takes the local strain, thermal aging parameters ( via  LMP), and initial nucleation state as inputs to predict the corresponding LTPH amount. This enables the continuous and high-resolution prediction of the LTPH distribution throughout the entire heterogeneous HAZ based on the local thermomechanical history obtained from welding process simulation ( e.g. , FEM).

sections.heading: Predicted hardening behavior and model validation
paragraphs: The LTPH amounts (ΔHV) predicted by the trained NN model are presented in Figures  8  and  9 . Figure  8  shows the predicted LTPH amounts for specimens without pre-existing carbide nuclei, while Figure  9  presents the corresponding predictions for specimens with pre-existing nuclei. In both cases, the model successfully reproduced the experimentally observed trends: the predicted LTPH amount increased monotonically with increasing strain and LMP. Furthermore, a clear and consistent difference in hardening magnitude between the two initial microstructural states was confirmed: the LTPH amount of specimens with pre-existing nuclei was consistently and significantly higher than that of specimens without nuclei, under identical thermal aging and strain conditions. Fig. 8 3D and 2D contour diagram between LTPH amount (ΔHV) and strain/LMP without carbide nuclei Fig. 9 3D and 2D contour diagram between LTPH amount (ΔHV) and strain/LMP with carbide nuclei

This agreement between the predicted trends and the experimental database (Figures  5  and  6 ) validates the predictive capability of the developed NN model and confirms that it has successfully learned the underlying physical relationships governing LTPH kinetics.

The NN model was trained on experimental LTPH data spanning 1 to 2000 hours at 300 °C to 500 °C. As demonstrated in our previous study, [ 10 ]  the measured LTPH kinetics inherently include competing phenomena such as recovery and recrystallization, particularly during the early stages of aging. Therefore, the model implicitly captures these competing effects through the experimental dataset rather than treating them as separate mechanisms. However, the current training data are limited to 2000 hours; for service periods beyond this range ( e.g. , > 40 years), extrapolation relies on the Larson–Miller parameterization. Phenomena such as precipitate coarsening or phase transformations that may occur over extremely long service periods are not explicitly accounted for in the current model and should be addressed in future work.

sections.heading: Neural network model validation results
paragraphs: The results of the five-fold cross-validation are summarized in Table  II . To rigorously address potential overfitting concerns, we employed 5-fold cross-validation, which provides a robust estimate of model generalizability by evaluating performance on multiple unseen subsets of the data. The model achieved an average  R 2  of 0.91 ± 0.02, indicating that the neural network explains approximately 91 pct of the variance in the experimental LTPH data. The average RMSE and MAE were 5.44 ± 0.70 and 4.16 ± 0.30 HV, respectively, which fall within acceptable ranges considering the typical experimental scatter of Vickers hardness measurements (approximately ± 5 HV). Figure  10  presents the cross-validation performance across the five folds. The red dashed lines indicate the mean values. As shown in Figure  10 (a), the  R 2  values range from 0.89 to 0.95, with all folds achieving scores above 0.88, demonstrating consistent predictive capability. Figures  10 (b) and (c) show the corresponding RMSE and MAE values, respectively. The small standard deviations across folds—approximately 2 pct for  R 2 , 13 pct for RMSE, and 7 pct for MAE—indicate that the model performance is stable and that it generalizes well to unseen data without significant overfitting. Fig. 10  Cross-validation performance of the neural network model

sections.heading: Full-Field Prediction of LTPH Distribution in Multi-Pass Welded HAZ Under Long-Term Aging
paragraphs: To assess the long-term integrity of welded structures, the developed NN-based LTPH prediction system was applied to a practical multi-pass welded joint. The objective was to quantitatively predict the spatial distribution of LTPH throughout the entire HAZ under simulated long-term aging conditions.

sections.heading: Finite element analysis of multi-pass welding process
paragraphs: A three-dimensional finite element method (FEM) model of the multi-pass welded joint was constructed using PATRAN software, as illustrated in Figure  11 . The mesh design was optimized to balance computational efficiency and numerical accuracy: finer meshes were employed in the weld metal (WM) and HAZ, while coarser grids were used in the base metal (BM) regions distant from the weld. The minimum element size in the vicinity of the WM was 0.5 mm to adequately capture the steep strain gradients induced by welding. Four-node generalized plane strain elements were used throughout the model. To prevent rigid body motion during analysis, a three-point constraint boundary condition was applied, as also shown in Figure  11 (a). Fig. 11 Simulation model of multi-pass welding sample (7 layer–13 pass)

The mesh size (minimum 0.5 mm in the HAZ region) was determined through a systematic mesh convergence study. Several mesh configurations with progressively refined element sizes were evaluated. The equivalent plastic strain at critical locations ( e.g. , fusion line, weld root) was compared. The 0.5 mm mesh was selected because it provided a reasonable balance between computational accuracy and cost; further refinement resulted in only minor changes in the predicted strain, confirming that the solution was sufficiently converged.

Temperature-dependent material properties used in the finite element analysis are summarized in Figure  12 . [ 2 ]  The thermo–elastic–plastic analysis was performed using the finite element program JWRIAN, [ 25 , 26 ]  which is specifically designed for predicting welding thermal history, residual stress, and deformation. Fig. 12 Temperature-dependent material properties of SUS316

In the thermal analysis, the moving heat source was modeled using a double ellipsoidal volumetric heat distribution. [ 25 ]  The peak temperature of the weld pool was controlled within the range of 1600 °C to 1800 °C to realistically simulate the fusion zone. The inter-pass temperature was maintained below 100 °C during the multi-pass welding sequence. Both thermal radiation and convection were considered as boundary conditions for heat loss.

The simulated results are presented in Figures  13  and  14 . Figure  13  shows the peak temperature distribution across the weld cross-section, while Figure  14  displays the corresponding equivalent plastic strain distribution. High equivalent plastic strain was observed predominantly near the fusion boundary and at the weld root region (bottom of the weld), indicating significant plastic deformation in these areas during the multi-pass welding process. Fig. 13 Simulated peak temperature in the cross-section Fig. 14 Simulated equivalent plastic strain in the cross-section

Although direct experimental validation of residual strain in the multi-pass HAZ was not performed in this study, the FEM model used (JWRIAN) has been extensively validated against X-ray diffraction and neutron diffraction measurements for similar austenitic stainless steel weld joints in previous studies. [ 25 , 26 ]

sections.heading: Prediction of as-welded hardness distribution
paragraphs: Prior to predicting the long-term aging effect, the as-welded hardness distribution in the HAZ was evaluated. Using the thermal and strain histories obtained from the FEM analysis, the initial hardness immediately after multi-pass welding was predicted by a model previously proposed by the authors that correlates changes in hardness with changes in dislocation density. [ 2 ]  The predicted as-welded hardness distribution in the HAZ is shown in Figure  15 . The hardness distribution (Figure  15 ) showed excellent spatial correlation with the predicted equivalent plastic strain (Figure  14 ). Specifically, the peak hardness region near the bottom surface and fusion line corresponded to the maximum predicted strain, while the base metal region corresponded to near-zero strain. Fig. 15 The predicted as-welded hardness distribution in HAZ

sections.heading: Prediction of LTPH distribution under long-term aging conditions
paragraphs: To evaluate the progressive hardening during long-term aging, the trained NN prediction system (Section  III–C ) was employed in conjunction with the FEM-calculated strain field. The FEM-calculated local equivalent plastic strain distribution was used as the strain input to the NN model. Thermal aging conditions were defined assuming a continuous service temperature of 300 °C for durations of 40, 60, and 100 years. The LMP was calculated accordingly for each aging condition.

For the prediction of hardening in the most susceptible regions of the multi-pass weld HAZ, a conservative assumption was adopted: the material was assumed to be in the state with pre-existing carbide nuclei (Φ = 1), which exhibits higher susceptibility to LTPH. This assumption ensures that the predicted hardening represents an upper-bound estimate for critical locations.

The hybrid FEM-NN-predicted spatial distributions of LTPH amount (ΔHV) throughout the HAZ after 40, 60, and 100 years of service at 300 °C are presented in Figure  16 . The key findings are as follows: First, after 40 years of operation, the predicted LTPH amount across the entire HAZ region remains below 40 HV. Second, the hardening distribution is spatially non-uniform, reflecting the underlying strain distribution from the welding process. Furthermore, with increasing service life (60 and 100 years), both the magnitude and the affected area of LTPH progressively expand. Fig. 16 Hybrid FEM-NN prediction of LTPH amount (ΔHV) distributions across the HAZ after 40, 60, and 100 years of service at 300 °C

It should be noted that direct experimental validation of the predicted LTPH distribution after 40 years of service is not yet available, as such long-term aging experiments are beyond the scope of this study. However, the as-welded hardness distribution (before aging) was experimentally validated in our previous work, [ 10 ]  confirming that the FEM strain field adequately captures the spatial trend of the initial hardness state.

sections.heading: Engineering significance
paragraphs: The hybrid FEM-NN method established in this study is the first to quantitatively predict the spatial distribution of LTPH amount (ΔHV) in multi-pass weld HAZ under long-term, low-temperature service conditions. The finding that the LTPH amount (ΔHV) remains below 40 HV after 40 years of operation provides a valuable quantitative benchmark for the integrity assessment of aged welded components.

Furthermore, the proposed LTPH prediction system provides a useful tool for life extension strategies for critical infrastructure, and may contribute to the realization of a low-carbon society by supporting the continued safe operation of existing plants beyond their original design life.

sections.heading: Synergistic Effects of Multi-Pass Welding-Induced Strain and Long-Term Aging on HAZ Hardening
paragraphs: The integrated approach combining FEM-based welding process simulation and NN-based LTPH prediction has revealed a critical insight: the spatial distribution of long-term precipitation hardening is fundamentally governed by the welding-induced plastic strain field.

As shown in Figure  16 , the regions exhibiting the highest LTPH after 40 to 100 years of service correspond closely to the areas of elevated equivalent plastic strain identified in the as-welded condition (Figure  14 ). This correlation is not coincidental but reflects a mechanistic synergy between prior deformation and subsequent precipitation kinetics. The increased dislocation density introduced by plastic straining provides preferential nucleation sites for M 23 C 6  carbides, as confirmed by TEM observations. [ 10 ]  This mechanism—where prior deformation accelerates subsequent precipitation—has been widely reported in microalloyed steels [ 27 ]  and is qualitatively consistent with observations in austenitic stainless steels. [ 28 ]  The present study provides quantitative evidence of this effect in the HAZ of SUS316 welds under long-term thermal aging conditions.

This finding has important implications: the susceptibility to long-term embrittlement caused by LTPH is essentially determined at the moment of multi-pass welding. HAZ regions that experience higher plastic strain, such as near the weld root and the fusion line, are more prone to severe precipitation hardening, regardless of the subsequent aging conditions.

sections.heading: Quantitative Benchmark for Integrity Assessment
paragraphs: The prediction that the LTPH amount remains below 40 HV after 40 years of service at 300 °C provides a quantitative, experimentally validated benchmark for plant life management. While a LTPH amount (ΔHV) of 40 HV is modest, it is unlikely to induce immediate embrittlement or stress corrosion cracking (SCC) initiation in the absence of other degradation factors. However, this benchmark must be interpreted with caution: Cumulative effects: LTPH does not occur in isolation. It superimposes upon the as-welded strain hardening (Figure  14 ) and potential dynamic strain aging. The total hardness increase in the most susceptible regions may therefore exceed 40 HV when all mechanisms are considered. Local  vs  global: The NN-predicted LTPH amount (ΔHV) of 40 HV represents a local, grain-scale hardening. Even if the macroscopic hardness increase appears modest, the local stress concentration at hard, precipitation-strengthened grain boundaries may be sufficient to promote micro-crack initiation under sustained tensile stress. Threshold behavior: The current study does not establish a critical hardening threshold for SCC initiation. Further research is required to correlate LTPH amount with actual SCC susceptibility under simulated nuclear power plant operating conditions.

sections.heading: Conservative Assumption of Pre-nucleation
paragraphs: In predicting the worst-case hardening for critical HAZ locations, a conservative assumption was adopted: the material was assumed to be in the state with pre-existing carbide nuclei (Φ = 1). This assumption is justified for the following reasons: Multi-pass welding often introduces initial sensitization or strain-induced carbide precipitation in the HAZ, which can serve as pre-existing carbide nuclei. Even without visible carbides, the high dislocation density in severely strained regions can effectively serve as nucleation sites, making the material functionally similar to the state with pre-existing carbide nuclei. From an applicability perspective, using an upper-bound estimate ensures that the predicted hardening does not underestimate the actual degree of degradation.

Nevertheless, it is acknowledged that not all HAZ locations will satisfy the condition with pre-existing carbide nuclei. The actual LTPH distribution may lie between the bounds defined by Φ = 0 and Φ = 1. The binary assumption (Φ = 0 or 1) simplifies what is in reality a continuous distribution of nucleation site densities in the HAZ microstructure. As confirmed by our previous EBSD and TEM characterization of as-welded HAZ regions, [ 10 ]  the nucleation condition can be more realistically described by a continuous parameter representing the density of potential nucleation sites ( ρ nuc ). In this context, the two binary cases correspond to limiting conditions: Φ = 0 represents the fully solution-annealed condition, while Φ = 1 represents the strain-sensitized condition.

For practical engineering assessments, it is recommended to assign Φ = 1 to HAZ regions within 0.5 mm of the fusion line and weld root, where the thermal cycle (peak temperature > 1100 °C) and plastic deformation ( ε  > 15 pct) are most severe. Conversely, for regions more than 2 mm from the fusion line (peak temperature < 900 °C,  ε  < 5 pct), Φ = 0 provides a lower bound estimate. Therefore, the actual LTPH distribution in partially sensitized regions ( e.g. , 0.5 to 2 mm from the fusion line) lies between these two bounds. Future work will develop a continuous prediction model for ρnuc based on local thermal history (peak temperature, cooling rate) and strain state, using physically informed interpolation between the two limiting cases.

sections.heading: Model Validation and Robustness
paragraphs: The developed NN model successfully captured the non-linear relationships between strain, thermal aging, and LTPH, as evidenced by the excellent agreement between predicted trends (Figures  8  and  9 ) and experimental data (Figures  5  and  6 ).

The use of 5-fold cross-validation provides a rigorous assessment of model generalizability. As shown in Table  II  and Figure  10 , the consistent  R 2  values across all five folds (0.89 to 0.95, mean 0.91 ± 0.02) demonstrate that the NN model does not exhibit significant overfitting. Overfitting occurs when a model learns noise specific to the training data rather than the underlying physical relationship, resulting in poor performance on unseen data. The small standard deviations across folds—approximately 2 pct for  R 2 , 13 pct for RMSE, and 7 pct for MAE—confirm that the model captures the true relationship between input parameters (strain, LMP, nucleation condition) and LTPH. This robustness can be attributed to two factors: (1) the NN model employs a simple architecture (radial basis function with a single hidden layer) with relatively few trainable parameters, and (2) the training data span a sufficiently wide range of experimental conditions (5 to 30 pct pre-strain, 300 °C to 500 °C, 1 to 2000 hours).

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work
paragraphs: Despite the successful development and validation of the hybrid FEM-NN prediction framework, several limitations must be acknowledged. These limitations are organized below according to their nature, and corresponding future work is proposed.

sections.heading: Extrapolation uncertainty
paragraphs: The NN model was trained on experimental data up to 2000 hours (approximately 3 months). The prediction for 40 to 100 years involves significant time extrapolation, relying on the validity of the LMP parameterization. The Larson-Miller parameter is derived from rate theory assuming thermally-activated processes following Arrhenius behavior. For precipitation kinetics, this parameter has been successfully applied to extrapolate creep rupture data over 4 to 5 orders of magnitude in time. [ 18 , 19 ]  The linearity of the ln(t)  vs.  1/T relationship was verified within our experimental temperature range (300 °C to 500 °C), with  R 2  = 0.97 for the nucleation-present condition.

sections.heading: Microstructural evolution coupling
paragraphs: The current model treats LTPH as an independent mechanism. As demonstrated in our previous study, [ 10 ]  the measured LTPH kinetics inherently include competing phenomena such as recovery, recrystallization, and precipitate coarsening, particularly during the early stages of aging. Therefore, the model implicitly captures these competing effects through the experimental dataset (aging 1 to 2000 hours at 300 °C to 500 °C), rather than treating them as separate mechanisms. However, two specific limitations should be noted. First, the current training data are limited to 2000 hours; for service periods beyond this range ( e.g. , > 40 years), extrapolation relies on the LMP parameterization. Second, phenomena that may occur over extremely long service periods, such as coarsening beyond the peak-aged condition or σ-phase formation, are not explicitly accounted for in the current model.

sections.heading: FEM-NN coupling uncertainties
paragraphs: The current framework assumes a deterministic mapping from FEM-simulated strain to LTPH output. Uncertainties in the FEM simulation ( e.g. , material properties, heat source modeling, mesh sensitivity, boundary conditions) and their propagation through the NN model have not been explicitly quantified. Nevertheless, the FEM strain field is used primarily as a spatial guide to map LTPH predictions across the HAZ, rather than as an absolute predictor. The NN model was trained on a wide strain range (5 to 30 pct) with smooth interpolation, which mitigates the impact of moderate strain inaccuracies.

A limitation of the current framework is the absence of direct experimental validation of the FEM-predicted strain field. However, the following points provide confidence in the simulation results. First, in our previous work, [ 10 ]  the predicted as-welded hardness distribution was quantitatively validated against experimental measurements. Since the as-welded hardness is directly governed by the strain history (dislocation density), this validation provides strong indirect evidence that the simulated strain field reliably captures the spatial trends across the HAZ. Second, the in-house FEM code JWRIAN has been extensively validated in the literature through comparisons with experimental measurements for various welding processes and material systems. [ 29 , 30 ]

sections.heading: Strain range limitation
paragraphs: The training database covers pre-strain levels up to 30 pct. HAZ regions experiencing strains beyond this range may exhibit different hardening behavior not captured by the current model, although the likelihood of pre-strain reaching 30 pct is very small. It has been reported that maximum welding strain of approximately 20 to 25 pct can be introduced into the multilayer welded HAZ of austenitic stainless steel. [ 31 , 32 ]

sections.heading: Generalization to other materials and conditions
paragraphs: The methodology and conclusions presented in this study are demonstrated on SUS316 austenitic stainless steel under the welding conditions described (7 layer, 13 pass, inter-pass temperature < 100 °C) and thermal aging in air. However, the overall FEM–NN framework is not inherently limited to these specific conditions. Changes in welding procedure: If the welding procedure changes ( e.g. , heat input, pass sequence, inter-pass temperature, or joint geometry), the FEM simulation can be directly re-performed under the new welding conditions. The resulting updated strain field can then be fed into the same trained NN model to obtain the corresponding LTPH prediction. Thus, the framework is transferable across different welding conditions without retraining the NN model, as long as the material remains SUS316 and the ranges of strain, temperature, and time remain within the training domain. Changes in base material: If the base material is changed ( e.g. , SUS304, SUS316L, or other austenitic stainless steels), the precipitation kinetics of M 23 C 6  may differ significantly due to variations in carbon, nitrogen, and molybdenum content. In such cases, the NN model would require retraining or fine-tuning with material-specific experimental data. Changes in service environment: This study considered only thermal aging in air. Application to nuclear reactor environments (neutron irradiation, primary water) [ 33 ,  34 – 35 ]  would require integration with irradiation and corrosion models, along with experimental validation.

sections.heading: Proposed future work
paragraphs: Based on the limitations identified above, the following future research directions are proposed: Uncertainty quantification: Future work will incorporate methods such as Monte Carlo dropout or ensemble neural networks to estimate prediction uncertainties, as well as global sensitivity analysis ( e.g. , Sobol indices) to identify the most influential input parameters. Sensitivity analyses and uncertainty quantification using methods such as Monte Carlo simulation or polynomial chaos expansion will be employed to establish confidence intervals for the final LTPH predictions. Direct strain field validation: Direct validation of the FEM-predicted strain field remains a future research direction. We plan to perform residual stress measurements ( e.g. , by X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction) to further validate the FEM predictions in subsequent studies. Model generalization: Expand the NN training database to include other austenitic stainless steel grades ( e.g. , SUS304, SUS316L) and welding processes. Coupled degradation modeling: Integrate LTPH prediction with SCC initiation models to establish a direct link between predicted hardening and cracking susceptibility. In situ  validation: Collaborate with plant operators to extract and characterize HAZ samples from components that have experienced long-term service, enabling direct validation of the predicted hardening evolution under actual operating conditions. Continuous nucleation model: Develop a continuous prediction model for  ρ nuc  based on local thermal history (peak temperature, cooling rate) and strain state, using physically informed interpolation between the two limiting cases (Φ = 0 and Φ = 1). Physically based coupling: Couple the NN model with physically-based precipitation kinetics models to enhance predictive robustness, particularly for extrapolation beyond the training range.

sections.heading: Implications for Multi-Scale Integrity Assessment and Service Extension
paragraphs: This study demonstrates an advance in structural integrity assessment: moving from empirical, post-factum evaluations to physics-based, preemptive predictions. By integrating process simulation (FEM), mechanistic understanding (TEM, hardness testing), and data-driven modeling (NN), a multi-scale framework capable of forecasting microstructural degradation across an entire weld HAZ over decades of service has been established. The practical implications are substantial: Design stage: The proposed methodology can identify regions in the HAZ that are intrinsically predisposed to long-term hardening, enabling mitigation strategies such as optimized welding parameters or post-weld heat treatment. Operation stage: The predicted spatial maps of LTPH (Figure  16 ) can inform risk-based inspection planning, focusing non-destructive examination on areas with the highest predicted hardening. Service extension: The developed prediction system provides a quantitative basis for assessing the remaining service life of aged welded components, supporting informed decision-making regarding plant operation and life extension.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study systematically investigated the low-temperature precipitation hardening (LTPH) phenomenon in the HAZ of multi-pass welded SUS316 austenitic stainless steel and established a hybrid FEM-NN-based quantitative prediction framework for long-term aging at nuclear reactor operating temperatures. The following conclusions are drawn: LTPH in the multi-pass weld HAZ of SUS316 steel is governed by intragranular M 23 C 6  carbide precipitation. The presence of pre-existing carbide nuclei and welding-induced plastic strain synergistically accelerates hardening kinetics. Systematic isothermal aging experiments (300 °C to 500 °C, 1 to 2000 hours) across pre-strain levels of 5 to 30 pct established a comprehensive LTPH database. The LMP exhibits a strong, non-linear correlation with hardening only when pre-existing carbide nuclei are present, highlighting the importance of nucleation condition. An RBF-NN model was successfully trained to accurately reproduce the non-linear dependence of LTPH amount (ΔHV) on local plastic strain, thermal history ( via  LMP), and initial nucleation condition, enabling predictions beyond the range of experimental conditions. Integration of the NN model with FEM simulation of multi-pass welding enabled spatial mapping of LTPH across the entire HAZ. Under the conservative assumption of pre-existing carbide nuclei, the predicted LTPH amount (ΔHV) remains below 40 HV throughout the HAZ after 40 years of service at 300 °C. The developed hybrid framework—combining FEM process simulation with an NN data-driven model—provides a quantitative foundation for integrity assessment, risk-informed inspection, and service life extension of welded components in nuclear power plants, demonstrating the effectiveness of this integrated approach for predicting long-term microstructural evolution.
